taxonomic_note: Legacy Master Plant Pool name Chamaesyce serpens is normalized to the current accepted Euphorbia name.
look_here_first: START at a stem NODE: E. serpens is often a creeping plant that produces ADVENTITIOUS ROOTS at nodes in contact with soil. Look for a BROAD fused white-to-pink triangular stipule scale. Independent photo-proved characters: glabrous THREE-LOBED capsules and a smooth SEED without strong crosswise ribs. Contrast E. prostrata's hairy capsule KEELS and strongly transversely ridged seed. The installed 'flowering mat' image actually shows a CYATHIUM macro, not a full-plant mat. Node-root macro has noncommercial/source-restricted reuse and must be kept out of public website copy.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays-local legacy Chamaesyce source; current Kew treats Chamaesyce serpens as a synonym of accepted Euphorbia serpens, native in Texas.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Installed for active visual learning; broader exact-county reconciliation deferred.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Euphorbia sect. Anisophyllum sandmat: opposite leaves, milky latex, tiny cyathia, and 3-lobed capsules; habit, stipules, hairiness, fruit, and seed are the most useful field structures.
morphology_keys.growth_form: Annual with slender taproot; stems strictly prostrate, frequently mat-forming and rooting at nodes, about 15–50 cm, glabrous. The local Williamson County treatment notes adventitious roots are commonly 1 or 2 per rooted node.
morphology_keys.leaves: Opposite; blades ovate, oblong, or orbiculate, usually 2–7(–9) × 2–6 mm; base asymmetric and rounded to subcordate; margins entire; apex rounded; surfaces glabrous and without a red blotch.
morphology_keys.stipules: Stipules are paired and fused across the node into conspicuous broad-deltate, white-to-pink membranous scales about 0.5–1(–1.2) mm; this fused scale is a major contrast with E. prostrata's upper-free/lower-fused pattern and E. villifera's distinct filiform stipules.
morphology_keys.cyathium: Cyathia solitary at distal nodes; 4 yellow oblong glands with small equal white-to-pink appendages forming a narrow rim at the gland edge.
morphology_keys.fruit: Capsule broadly ovoid, oblate, or subglobose, about 1.3–1.4 × 1.3–1.7 mm, glabrous.
morphology_keys.seed: Seeds white to gray or light pink, ovoid, bluntly 3–4 angled in cross section, about 0.7–1.1 × 0.4–0.7 mm, smooth.
best_field_traits: Strictly prostrate, low spreading annual with small opposite rounded leaves; not all photographed flower macros show mat habit.
Stems often put out adventitious ROOTS where nodes touch ground; evidence exists in historical research photo but that CC BY-NC-SA item is NOT eligible for public web distribution.
Broad triangular white-to-pink STIPULE SCALES are fused across nodes, unlike prostrata's partly free narrow stipules.
Stems and fruit essentially GLABROUS (without conspicuous hairs).
Three-lobed glabrous capsule around 1.3–1.7 mm across.
Seeds approximately 0.7–1.1 mm with no strong transverse ridges; original 1 mm scale source photo covers surface.
Tiny cyathia with dark nectar glands and small white appendages; don't mistake them for four separate petals.
Texas-native state-level recognition does not resolve this project's county target-zone hold.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Against E. prostrata: check a node first—serpens frequently roots there and has fused broad-deltate stipule scales; prostrata does not root at nodes and has an upper-free/lower-fused stipule pattern. Serpens is also glabrous with glabrous capsules and smooth seeds, while prostrata is crisped-villous with hairy capsule keels and ridged seeds. Against E. villifera, serpens is a glabrous rooted mat with fused scales; villifera is usually erect/ascending with distinct filiform stipules and papillate surfaces.
crew_field_protocol: Recognize a tiny creeping Euphorbia by opposite small leaves; don't guess from red spots.
Look at multiple SOIL-CONTACT nodes for rooting and inspect pale stipules from both stem sides.
Photograph a 3-lobed fruit, noting whether the raised KEELS are hairy or glabrous.
Photograph a released mature SEED with 1–2 mm ruler, compare transverse ridges.
If only a low mat/flower photo, identify to sandmat group rather than force species.

lookalike_matrix.Euphorbia serpens: strictly prostrate, often mat-forming and rooting at nodes
frequently roots at nodes; often 1–2 adventitious roots per rooted node
lookalike_matrix.Euphorbia villifera: usually erect/ascending; node-rooting is not the defining growth pattern

lookalike_matrix.Euphorbia serpens: pairs connate into conspicuous broad-deltate membranous scales
lookalike_matrix.Euphorbia prostrata: upper-side pair free; lower-side pair fused across node
crisped-villous on stems/leaves; fruit hairy on keels
triangular-subulate, lower side connate/upper side often distinct

comparisons.key_distinctions: The fastest split is a node: adventitious root + fused deltate stipule scale strongly favors E. serpens. Complete glabrousness, a glabrous capsule, and a smooth seed provide independent confirmation.
crew_key: Prostrata: HAIRY capsule keels + STRONGLY RIDGED seeds.
Serpens: GLABROUS capsule + SMOOTH seed without strong crosswise ribs.
Prostrata: upper-side stipules free and lower fused; serpens: broad, fused triangular scales.
Serpens OFTEN roots at contact nodes, prostrata usually does not. Absence of a root in ONE view is not proof.
Without capsule or seed, label E. prostrata–serpens group.
unreliable_traits: Red leaf spots (variable even in E. maculata)
Seed apparent size on phone screen without real scale

items.label: Not a whole mat: tiny Euphorbia cyathium
items.image_role: Real macro of a tiny flower-like cyathium with four purple glands and white appendages
items.creator: Rahooda
items.caption: This is a close-up of a single CYATHIUM, NOT a whole mat. Four dark glands with small white petal-like appendages surround highly reduced flowers; these are not four ordinary petals.
items.why_it_matters: Crew learns to distinguish the whole reproductive cup from a three-lobed fruit.

items.label: The broad fused stipule scale
items.image_role: Microscopic node with wide pale/pink fused triangular membranous scale
items.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
items.caption: The pale/pink membrane wraps across the node like one broad triangular scale; the green stem is smooth-looking. The original 2 mm photo bar is preserved. This is not a root.
items.why_it_matters: The fused broad-deltate stipules support E. serpens more than prostrata's narrow, partly free ones.

items.label: Glabrous three-lobed capsule
items.image_role: Actual ripe-looking capsule with smooth surfaces and visible lobe grooves
items.creator: Rahooda
items.caption: The green capsule has three rounded lobes and appears completely glabrous. Compare the sharp projecting hairs on prostrata's capsule keel.
items.why_it_matters: One of the simplest small-character distinctions using a real macro.

items.label: Smooth-looking mature seed
items.image_role: Single genuine yellowish seed without strong repeated transverse ridges
items.creator: Stefan.lefnaer
items.caption: Unlike E. prostrata's seed, this one has no conspicuous crosswise RIBS. Fine surface texture is visible; 'smooth' here means lacking the strong transverse ridges, not perfectly glasslike. Source original scale bar 1 mm.
items.why_it_matters: Makes the seed comparison honest at real photographic resolution.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Matted sandmat: FUSED stipule, SMOOTH fruit and seed
steps: Find a broad fused membranous stipule scale at a leaf node.
Compare the distinctly smooth three-lobed capsule with E. prostrata's hairy capsule keels.
Find the mature smoothish seed: lacks repeated bold transverse ridges shown in the prostrata macro.
Check for little adventitious roots at real soil-contact nodes; the original study photo exists but is NOT a public training illustration.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Glabrous capsule, mature seed without strong crosswise ribs and broad fused stipule scale support E. serpens.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: The strongest node-root image is rights restricted; do not present it as a public photo. Absence of strong seed ridges does not mean the photo must look featureless.
